title: tries, prefix trees, and string dictionaries
concepts: A trie stores keys by shared prefixes, with each edge representing one character or symbol and each node representing a prefix state.
Lookup and insertion take time proportional to key length rather than the number of stored keys, while memory depends on how many distinct prefix nodes and child links are stored.
A terminal marker distinguishes a complete key from a prefix that merely leads to longer keys; a node may be both terminal and have children.

An array of child references gives fast fixed-alphabet lookup but reserves space per possible symbol, while hash maps or sorted child collections trade overhead for sparse alphabets or ordered traversal.
Prefix queries can enumerate all keys below a node; wildcard or pattern search branches over multiple children and may visit many trie states.
Deletion clears terminal state and may prune nodes that no longer lead to any key, but shared prefixes must remain while another stored key uses them.
A trie is useful for prefix-heavy workloads, autocomplete-like lookup, and lexicographic search; a hash set is often more memory-efficient for exact lookup alone.
Compressed radix tries merge chains of single-child nodes, while binary tries branch on bits and support XOR-related queries; these are distinct representations with different alphabets.
